Complementary information — The question is underspecified, allowing answers about first British contact (1769), formal annexation (1840), or key steps (treaty signing, sovereignty proclamation).

The evidence provides complementary facets of the British arrival: d3 and d8 describe the first British explorer James Cook's arrival in 1769 [d3, d8], while d1, d2, d4, and d10 focus on the formal establishment of British sovereignty and annexation in 1840, detailing the Treaty of Waitangi (6 February 1840) and the proclamation of sovereignty (21 May 1840) [d1, d2, d4, d10]. Other docs add context about pre-1840 settlers [d5] and the 1839 diplomatic mission [d9].

The final answer combines these non-contradictory facets: the first British arrival was in 1769, but the formal process of British coming to rule New Zealand culminated in 1840 with the Treaty of Waitangi and the proclamation of sovereignty.

British contact with New Zealand began with the arrival of explorer Captain James Cook in October 1769 [d3, d8]. The formal process of British annexation occurred in 1840, marked by the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi on 6 February 1840 [d2, d4, d10] and Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson's proclamation of British sovereignty on 21 May 1840 [d1, d2]. Therefore, while British individuals had visited earlier, the British Crown established sovereignty over New Zealand in 1840 [d4, d10].
